title: Make the daily puzzle a 3×3 city with visible buildings
summary: Requested by Lauren in her ux-001 review, then revised after her preview: the play area is a clearly bordered 3×3 board, and every height she types draws a building, with a worked example and per-side sightlines to explain the edge numbers. One commit, in brainteaser.js.

decision.subject: Homepage · daily brain teaser
decision.context: Revised from your feedback: the board is now clearly 3×3 (edge numbers sit outside it), typed heights appear as buildings, and tapping an edge number lights up what you can see from that side. Still easy: only 12 possible 3×3 grids.

options.label: Ship it
options.effect: Reviewed deployment to everyone, then compare solve rates before and after

options.label: Keep 4×4
options.effect: Leave the puzzle as it is

options.label: Other
options.effect: Tell me what you want instead

steps: Open the homepage (the preview starts as a new visitor, so the puzzle appears).
Current: a 4×4 grid of number boxes, with the edge numbers in matching boxes.

Proposed: a bordered 3×3 board. Type heights 1–3 and watch the buildings appear; tap an edge number to see which buildings are visible from that side; a full row or column turns its edge numbers green or red.

hypothesis: A smaller grid takes less time, so more of the visitors who see the puzzle will finish it rather than skip or close it.

evidence.statement: With the 4×4 grid, 6 of 89 new visitors and 2 of 18 returning visitors solved the puzzle; 11 new visitors used Skip.
evidence.source: GA4 property 546626239 · brainteaser_played, brainteaser_skipped · last 28 days

evidence.statement: The generator already works for any size; only two instruction lines hard-coded 1–4. All 200 test puzzles generated at 3×3 were valid. The new board, buildings, sightlines and clue colours were checked in a simulated browser, and a full correct solution is still accepted.
A 3×3 puzzle may feel too easy to be satisfying, which could lower repeat interest. Not measured.
Seeing the buildings may make the edge numbers easier to understand for first-time players, so more of them try the puzzle instead of skipping. Not measured.

prediction.expectedEffect: More solves per visitor who sees the puzzle. No size is claimed.
prediction.uncertainty: High: under 20 solves a month today, and the overlay closes (×, Escape, outside click) are not tracked, so the base rate is incomplete.

successMetric.definition: Solves (brainteaser_played) divided by visitors shown the puzzle.
guardrails: Share of visitors who reach a practice question
successMetric.measurementPlan: Before/after over 4+ weeks each, reported as observational. Tracking puzzle impressions and closes first would give a proper denominator.
